# Making visuals A visual is a small, self-contained HTML (or SVG) widget that renders inline in the conversation, in a rounded card the width of the reply (about 640–760 px on desktop, 360 px on a phone). Its job is to build intuition: the reader should *play* with it and see the idea move. A good one beats three paragraphs. ## When to make one - The user asks to see, visualize, explain visually, or build intuition for something. - A concept has a knob worth turning: a parameter whose effect is the point (a gap, a speed, a current, a step size, a learning rate). - Data with shape: a trend, a distribution, a comparison. - A mechanism with moving parts: fields, waves, orbits, gradients, queues, algorithms stepping. Not for: short factual answers, code changes, lists, or anything a sentence or a table says just as well. For architecture boxes-and-arrows, use Diagram instead. One visual per idea; a long explanation may have two or three, each introduced by a sentence. ## Shape of a great widget 1. **Controls on top**: one to three. A labelled slider with its live value on the right, a checkbox toggle, or a segmented button pair ("Lab view | Ride with the electrons"). 2. **The picture**: an SVG or canvas that redraws when a control moves. Label things *in* the picture (plate, mirror, N, S, "inside: only n·λ/2 = d") rather than in a legend. 3. **Stat tiles at the bottom**: two to four numbers that change with the controls ("modes allowed inside: 8 of 12", "slope here: −0.894"). Short label, big value. 4. Optional one-line caption under the picture. The explanation itself goes in your reply text, not inside the widget. Make it interactive: something to drag, slide, toggle or step. Animate only when motion *is* the idea (fluctuations, flow, a wave) and keep it gentle. ## The kit (already styled; use these classes) ```html
4.0 units
dashed = forbidden modes
modes allowed inside
8 of 12
relative pull ∝ 1/d⁴
1.00×
``` Also: `.stack`, `.row`, `.muted`, `.mono`, `.legend` (`label`), `.btn` / `.btn.on`, `select`. ## Colour and type: always CSS variables The card follows the app's light or dark theme, so never hard-code colours. - Text `var(--fg)`, secondary `var(--muted)`, faint labels `var(--faint)`. - Lines, grids, axes `var(--line)` / `var(--line-strong)`. Tile and panel fill `var(--surface)`, deeper wells `var(--well)`. - Series and highlights `var(--c1)` … `var(--c8)` (green, blue, orange, purple, yellow, pink, teal, grey). Use two or three, each with a meaning, and keep it consistent across the widget. - `var(--accent)` is Frog green; `--good`, `--bad`, `--warn` for status. - **The background is transparent**: never paint `body`, the root or the SVG with a background colour. The card provides the canvas (true black in dark mode). - In SVG use `fill="var(--c2)"` or `style="stroke:var(--line)"`. In canvas read the values once: `const css = getComputedStyle(document.documentElement); const c2 = css.getPropertyValue('--c2').trim();`, and re-read on `matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').addEventListener('change', …)`. - Fonts are IBM Plex Sans / Plex Mono via `var(--font)` / `var(--mono)`; body text is 14 px. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for changing numbers (tiles already do). ## Rules of the sandbox - Send a **fragment**: no ``, ``, `` or ``. Put `

Design a widget that builds intuition for the Fourier transform. Best approach: a signal (sum of a few sine waves) with a "probe frequency" slider — a rotating phasor at frequency f, and the signal multiplied by it, showing the integral (center of mass). Classic: "winding" the signal around a circle at probe frequency, and the center of mass magnitude is the Fourier transform magnitude. I'll build: - Top: time-domain signal (sum of sines with adjustable amplitudes/freqs). - Middle: winding — the signal plotted as complex curve e^{-2πi f t}·x(t), trail of points. - Bottom: the spectrum |X(f)| with a marker at current probe frequency. Controls: probe frequency slider, toggle animate (winding rotation grows), maybe toggles for the components. Simplest and most instructive: pick a fixed signal = sum of 3 sines. Slider: probe frequency f. Show winding with the winding trail, plus a "radius" (center of mass) indicator. Also show spectrum line with marker, computed numerically. Also add toggles: animate the winding so the user sees the trail draw over time. Maybe simpler: compute full winding curve statically and show the center-of-mass dot. Animate as "wind up" progress — that's nice. Let me write it carefully. Math: x(t) for t in [0,1] (say). components: - 2 Hz sine amplitude 1 - 5 Hz sine amplitude 0.6 - 9 Hz sine amplitude 0.35 Use g(t) = e^{-2πi f t}, product curve p(t) = x(t)·g(t) drawn in complex plane. Center of mass = mean of p over t. |com| gives |X(f)| scaled. Winding curve: x(t) real → p(t) = x(t)(cos(-2πft), sin(-2πft)) — a rose-like curve. Draw in SVG with viewBox 0 0 680 420 maybe. Layout: left panel = time signal (small, top-left), right = winding circle, bottom = spectrum. Maybe better: stack three panels: 1. time domain plot: 680x100 2. winding circle: centered, ~240x240 on the left, with the spectrum on the right. 3. spectrum: 680x110. Let me do: - Panel A (time signal): x from 20..660, y 20..110. - Panel B (winding): circle center (200, 250), radius 95. - Panel C (spectrum): x 20..660, y 350..450. Total viewBox 680x470. Animate: draw progress u from 0→1 with requestAnimationFrame, trail from 0 to u. Center of mass accumulates. When u hits 1, hold, then restart? Better: continuous loop slowly, or make animation optional with a play toggle. Default: animate on, looping with a pause. Actually to keep it simple and reduce risk: animate the winding progress on loop (2.5s draw, 1s hold). Reduced motion → static full. Spectrum computed numerically over f range 0..12 Hz, 240 samples. Marker line at probe f. Also show spectrum curve normalized to max. Tiles: |X(f)| at probe (relative), peak frequency, "energy captured" percentage. Let me define signal components with amplitudes so spectrum peaks: at 2, 5, 9 Hz. Note: real signal → |X(f)| has peaks at ±f, but we're only scanning positive f, and using one-sided convention where the magnitude at f>0 is A/2 (for the mean of x·e^{-2πift}). Also, x(t) should include maybe a DC? no. Also note the winding at f=0 → the curve collapses onto the real axis (a horizontal line), and center of mass = mean = 0. That's fine and instructive. Add a second control: "component toggles"? Might complicate. Instead: slider for probe frequency + toggle "animate" + segmented control choosing the signal preset? Maybe two presets: "three tones" and "square-ish". Hmm, keep it focused: one signal, one knob (probe frequency), plus animation toggle. Maybe add a "hold" toggle... no. Actually a nice second knob: amplitude of one component to see peak height change. Eh — keep restraint. I'll add a segmented control for "signal": tones / pulse? The pulse (single Gaussian-ish bump) shows a broad flat spectrum — great contrast. Let's add signal presets: - "three tones": 2,5,9 Hz sines - "one pulse": a bump at t=0.5 width 0.06 → spectrum flat/wide. - maybe "square": square wave → odd harmonics 1,3,5,7... Three presets via seg buttons. Good, each tells something. Let me code. Signal functions (t in [0,1]): tones: 1.0*sin(2π*2t) + 0.6*sin(2π*5t) + 0.35*sin(2π*9t) square: sum over odd k=1,3,5,7,9 of (1/k) sin(2π k t) — that's a square-ish wave (sawtooth-like). Actually sum sin(2πkt)/k gives square wave with 1/k amplitudes for odd harmonics. pulse: exp(-((t-0.5)/0.05)^2) - mean... should subtract mean to keep mean 0? A Gaussian bump has nonzero mean; DC component appears at f=0 which is fine (shows DC). Keep it, shows a DC peak. Normalize signal to max abs 1 for display. Compute spectrum: for f in 0..12 step: X(f) = mean over samples of x(t)*e^{-2πift}, magnitude. Note for negative? Only positive. Winding curve: p(t) = (x(t)cos(2πft), -x(t) sin(2πft))? Since e^{-2πift} = cos - i sin. In SVG y is flipped, so plot (Re, -Im) → y down = -Im... let's just map complex (re, im) to screen (cx + s*re, cy - s*im). Then im = -x sin(2πft). Fine. Scale: max |x| = 1, so curve fits radius s. Time plot: draw x(t) vs t. Spectrum plot: curve of |X(f)| normalized by max over the scan; marker at probe. Center of mass: accumulate sum over t samples up to u. Compute mean p = (1/N)*Σ p(t). Magnitude → tile. Tiles: - "captured amplitude |X(f)|" = value normalized to max as % or absolute. item.text:
Now the explanation. Keep it tight, casual, direct. Explain the winding intuition, then the three mental models, then what FT actually is, then caveats. Reference the widget.

Key points:
1. Winding: multiply by e^{-i2πft} and average = how much of x oscillates at f. It's a matched filter / correlation. The center of mass is the answer.
2. Only exact resonance leaves a nonzero CoM (for periodic signals); off-resonance winds around evenly and cancels.
3. The spectrum panel is just doing this for every f.
4. Real FT = complex exponential, real signals give conjugate symmetry, magnitude = amplitude/2, phase = starting angle.
5. Time domain is the FT; it's a change of basis — delta in time = flat in freq (the pulse preset shows this).
6. Uncertainty: narrow pulse = broad spectrum (slide probe with pulse and see it never be narrow).
7. Try: square wave — odd harmonics, 1/k amplitudes, and Gibbs ringing.
8. Drag f to 4.5 and watch capture → 0. Between tones.
9. Convolution/multiplication theorem — maybe mention briefly.
10. Practical: FFT is just this sampled at N points, O(N log N).

Also note the tile "strongest peak at" changes with signal.

Mention limitations: they should play. Maybe suggest: with "three tones", drag the probe slowly from 0 to 12 and watch the trail go from messy blob → clean one-loop-ish shape → blob.

Keep it concise but substantive. Maybe use a small "try this" list. And offer to go deeper (filters, DFT bin spacing, sampling/aliasing) — but not as prose question; per instructions, questions to Cam should be clickable. That's for the chief-of-staff role but general. I could just offer a follow-up via sendPrompt... Instructions say use sendPrompt sparingly for "Go deeper". I'll skip extra buttons and just say what's next. Actually I can offer options as text? The memory says present questions as clickable. But this is a light offer. I'll just end with a short line, no question mark question. Or use Present actions? Probably overkill. Keep it simple — one line offering to do aliasing/sampling next.

Length: medium. Use headers sparingly.

The whole thing is one idea: **winding a signal around a circle and seeing where its center of mass lands.**

Take x(t), multiply by a rotating unit vector at frequency f, and the result traces a curve in the plane. Average that curve over the interval — the center of mass. That average *is* the Fourier transform at f.

Why it works: if x already oscillates at exactly f, the rotation cancels it and every point pushes the same direction — the curve collapses onto a half-line, and the CoM sits far out. If f is wrong, the curve wraps evenly around the circle and the pushes cancel to nothing. The transform is a **matched filter**: "how much of my signal is this exact spiral?"

That's the middle panel. The right panel is the same calculation run for every f — the spectrum is just the winding done 240 times. In the widget, drag the probe with "three tones" and watch:

- probe on 2.0 → the trail is a single smooth loop, the CoM ring is big
- probe at 3.5 (between tones) → the trail scribbles all around the circle, CoM shrinks to nearly zero
- probe at 9.0 → small but nonzero: that third tone has amplitude 0.35

**Three things the winding view gives you for free:**

1. **Amplitude is radius, phase is angle.** The CoM is complex. Its distance from center is how much of that frequency is present; its direction is where in the cycle that component starts. Drag the probe slightly off a peak and the CoM slides *around* the circle while shrinking — that's phase rotating, which is why filters delay signals.

2. **Time and frequency are the same information, rotated.** Switch to "one pulse": a narrow Gaussian in time becomes a broad Gaussian in frequency. You can't have both narrow — that's the uncertainty principle, not a mystical claim. A delta function is flat across all frequencies; a pure sine is a delta in frequency. Nothing is lost in the transform, just viewed along a different axis.

3. **Sharp corners need infinite frequencies.** The "square wave" preset is the sum of odd harmonics at 1/k amplitude. Its spectrum shows peaks at 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 Hz falling off like 1/f — and those ringing overshoots at the corners (Gibbs) are the price of truncating that infinite series.

**What the usual formula is doing:**

$$X(f) = \int x(t)\, e^{-2\pi i f t}\, dt$$

That `e^{-2πift}` is the rotating vector, the integral is the average, and `i` is what lets the two directions (real/imag) stay separate instead of collapsing. Real signals satisfy X(−f) = X(f)\*, so people plot only half the spectrum; and a sine of amplitude A shows up as peaks of height A/2 at ±f, which is why FFT magnitudes look half-sized.

Practically: the FFT isn't a different transform, it's this same sum evaluated at N equally spaced frequencies, exploiting symmetry so it costs N log N instead of N². And the reason it's everywhere is that convolution in time is multiplication in frequency — filters, image blur, audio EQ are all "multiply the spectrum, transform back."

Want to go deeper on one branch — aliasing and the sampling theorem, or the convolution theorem with a live filter you can drag?
